Turn a small JavaScript schema into a real working form.

This page tells the story behind ks-web-components: a reusable Web Component layer where JavaScript describes the fields, the component system builds the UI, and the browser renders the final form. The two screenshots below show that journey from configuration to visible output.

01 · The story

Why this project exists

A form should not require the same HTML, CSS and event wiring to be repeated every time. The project moves that repetitive work into reusable custom elements and configuration. Instead of thinking “build three input boxes”, the developer can think “these are my fields and this is their layout”.

From description → component → interface

The important idea is separation of responsibility. A page supplies a schema. The component layer interprets that schema and composes smaller controls. The browser then receives ordinary HTML elements and renders the final interface.

The screenshot is not the starting point — it is the result of a small configuration being interpreted by the component system.

UI

What the repository provides

The repository describes itself as a zero-dependency Custom HTML Web Component and Tailwind CSS token library for high-performance forms and tables. It includes custom elements, schema-driven form support, token registries, a Vite build, CLI scaffolding, documentation and versioned test examples.

03 · How it works

The small idea behind the big UI

Think of the example as a four-stage pipeline.

STEP 01
Define columnsThe JavaScript starts with field names such as Name, Mobile and Email.
STEP 02
Create schemacolumns.map(...) converts each field into a configuration object.
STEP 03
Compose componentA custom element such as ks-horizontal-form receives the schema/options.
STEP 04
Render UIThe component creates the controls and the browser paints the final form.
// Simplified story represented by the screenshot
const columns = ["Name", "Mobile", "Email"];

const formSchema = columns.map(column => ({
  labelText: column,
  inputType: column === "Email" ? "email" : "text",
  theme: "split-30-70"
}));

const form = document.createElement("ks-horizontal-form");
form._options = formSchema;
document.body.appendChild(form);
04 · Repository map

What is actually inside the repo?

The repository is more than a collection of custom tags. It combines component source, versioned test pages, build tooling, generated documentation and a small CLI into one reusable package.

ks-web-components/ ├── webComponents/ component implementations ├── test/ browser test playgrounds │ ├── v1 … v9/ versioned examples │ └── v4/ base control tests ├── docs/ documentation + built assets ├── dist/ distribution/build area ├── viteBuild/ build orchestration helpers ├── bin/ CLI entry point ├── index.js package/component exports ├── vite.config.js Vite library build ├── package.json scripts + package metadata ├── README.md project overview ├── DEV.md developer guide ├── HOWTO.md usage tutorials ├── ARCHITECTURE.md component architecture └── DETAILS.md schema-driven form deep dive
01

Component layer

Custom HTML elements form the low-level UI layer. The architecture document describes these elements as the component layer consumed by higher-level systems such as jsTableBuilderViews.

02

Token layer

Tailwind-oriented token registries provide consistent classes for table cell text, numeric values, bold totals, centered content and other visual rules.

03

Build & distribution

Vite is used for the library build. The configuration determines the highest component version and writes the build into a versioned docs/dist location.

05 · V4 test lab

Why the testing folder matters

The test/v4 area is a practical browser playground. The current public repository exposes separate pages for label, input, button, checkbox, vertical-form and JS-options tests, with an index page linking them together.

⌁

Input

Checks themes, HTML input types, disabled/read-only/autofocus states, values and custom classes.

□

Button + Checkbox

Provides focused examples for atomic controls before they are composed into larger interfaces.

↔

Vertical Form

Demonstrates composition: multiple controls can be arranged into a reusable higher-level form pattern.

06 · Local verification

How to check the project yourself

Use the repository as the source of truth, then open the browser test page and compare the rendered output with the schema/code.

01

Install dependencies

From the repository root, run npm install.

02

Start the development server

The package defines npm run dev as the Vite development command. Your screenshot is using http://localhost:3000/test/v4/, so keep the port used by your local setup.

03

Open the v4 test

Visit /test/v4/. The repository's v4 index links to the individual control examples.

04

Change the input/schema

Update the JavaScript configuration — for example the columns array or form schema — and refresh the browser to see how the rendered component changes.

05

Build the library when needed

The package also defines npm run build, which runs the Vite library build described in vite.config.js.

07 · Architecture in one sentence

Configuration is the language; components are the engine.

A developer supplies intent through a small schema, the custom-element layer turns that intent into composed controls, and the browser produces a consistent interface. That is the core story visible in your screenshots.

Reusable

Move repeated form/control markup into custom elements and reuse the same behavior across pages.

Composable

Atomic controls can be assembled into higher-level patterns such as horizontal and vertical forms.

Consistent

Shared themes and Tailwind token mappings keep visual rules centralized instead of scattered across pages.
